sources.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge Part II Mathematical Tripos; author-hosted PDF)
sources.locator: Chapter 2 Sections 2.1 and 2.6-2.6.2, printed pages 10-13 and 37-42 (PDF pages 17-20 and 44-49); Chapter 3 Section 3.2.1, printed pages 52-53 (PDF page 59)

contents.name: Section 2.1, printed pages 10-12: first variation of the action with fixed endpoints and derivation of Lagrange's equations
contents.support: The lemma extends the same fixed-endpoint family calculus one order further, with the compact-interval conventions of that section.

contents.name: Section 2.1, printed page 12: the principle of least action is a misnomer; the proof only requires delta S=0, and the true path may be either a minimum or a saddle point
contents.support: The proposition computes the second variation of the oscillator action and exhibits both signs beyond T=pi/omega, realising the minimum-or-saddle alternative quantitatively.

contents.name: Section 2.6, printed pages 37-40: small oscillations about equilibrium; normal modes as eigenvectors of the linearised system, each ringing at a single frequency
contents.support: The proposition identifies the eigenvectors and frequencies of the two-mass system and proves the decoupling into two single-frequency scalar oscillators.

contents.name: Section 2.6.1, printed pages 41-42: worked double-pendulum normal modes
contents.reason: The worked example is a different mechanical system (double pendulum); the verification page computes the two-mass three-spring system instead, which is the design's E19 claim, so no item consumes the double-pendulum computation.

contents.name: Section 3.2.1, printed pages 52-53: parallel-axis claim (3.25) with the expansion proof (3.26), the linear terms vanishing in the centre-of-mass frame
contents.support: The theorem proves the same identity for a centred bounded finite Borel measure, replacing the discrete sums by Lebesgue integrals under the finiteness hypotheses.

contents.name: Section 3.2.1, printed page 53: worked parallel-axis evaluations for the rod and the disc
contents.reason: These are routine evaluations of the same formula at particular shapes and are not part of the design's E19 claims; the page's companion example instead checks the identity on two point masses.

sources.locator: Chapter 1 Section 1.2 Eq. (1.18), printed page 6 of Chapter 1 (PDF page 10); Chapter 3 Section 3.2 Eq. (3.18), printed pages 3-4 of Chapter 3 (PDF pages 36-37); Chapter 4 Section 4.2 Eqs. (4.27)-(4.29), printed pages 6-7 of Chapter 4 (PDF pages 60-61); Chapter 5 Section 5.1 Eqs. (5.1)-(5.3), printed pages 1-2 of Chapter 5 (PDF pages 87-88); Chapter 6 Section 6.1 Eqs. (6.1)-(6.13), printed pages 1-4 of Chapter 6 (PDF pages 125-128)

contents.name: Chapter 1 Section 1.2, Eq. (1.18), printed page 6 of Chapter 1: the pendulum equation mR theta'' = -mg sin theta for a point mass on a light rod
contents.support: The proposition takes exactly this second-order equation as the explicit model, in the normalised first-order form theta''=-omega^2 sin theta.

contents.name: Chapter 3 Section 3.2, Eq. (3.18), printed pages 3-4 of Chapter 3: linearisation of the equation of motion about a fixed point via a linear Taylor expansion of the effective force
contents.support: The proposition carries out the same linearisation for the pendulum field and adds the quantitative finite-time error bound with the cubic remainder.

contents.name: Chapter 4 Section 4.2, Eqs. (4.27)-(4.29), printed pages 6-7 of Chapter 4: the axis-shift theorem I'_{jj'}=I_{jj'}+M(delta_{jj'} d^2 - d_j d_{j'}) with the shift vector d, and the special case d perpendicular to a principal axis
contents.support: This is an independent treatment of the parallel-axis identity; the theorem reconstructs it measure-theoretically for centred mass distributions with explicit finiteness hypotheses.

contents.name: Chapter 5 Section 5.1, Eqs. (5.1)-(5.3), printed pages 1-2 of Chapter 5: the harmonic oscillator equation and its general two-constant solution u cos(omega t)+v sin(omega t)
contents.support: The proposition uses the classification of the oscillator solutions (via the run's own classification theorem) to identify the one-dimensional Dirichlet solution space at T=n pi/omega.

contents.name: Chapter 6 Section 6.1, Eqs. (6.1)-(6.13), printed pages 1-4 of Chapter 6: two coupled linear oscillators, the characteristic equation, and the symmetric case with in-phase soft mode omega_-^2=kappa_L/m and anti-phase hard mode
contents.support: The proposition specialises the general two-oscillator calculation to equal masses and symmetric outer springs and proves the eigenrelations and decoupling rigorously.

contents.name: Chapter 6 Section 6.2, printed pages 4 onwards: N coupled oscillators and the general eigenfrequency problem
contents.reason: The verification page is scoped to the two-mass system of E19; the general N-oscillator spectral theory is not part of the assigned section and no item consumes it.

contents.name: Chapter 3 Section 3.3, Eqs. (3.24)-(3.25), printed pages 4-5 of Chapter 3: Hamiltonian one-dimensional systems and the first-integral energy equation
contents.reason: The energy-first-integral route is not used by the verification items, which work with the Euler-Lagrange and linearisation routes; the design's E19 claims do not reference it.

sources.title: D. Cline, Variational Principles in Classical Mechanics (2nd edition, University of Rochester River Campus Libraries, open textbook, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)
sources.locator: Chapter 5 Sections 5.1-5.2, pages 143-147 of the PDF pagination; Chapter 14 Sections 14.2-14.3, pages 488-492 of the PDF pagination

contents.name: Section 5.1, page 143 of the PDF pagination: introduction to the calculus of variations and the action integral
contents.support: The definition materialises the fixed-endpoint family q+epsilon eta of that section and adds the second derivative at zero as a well-defined new object.

contents.name: Section 5.2, pages 144-147 of the PDF pagination: Euler's differential equation from the stationarity condition, with the remark that the stationary value could be either a maximum or a minimum
contents.support: The proposition confirms the maximum-or-minimum alternative for the oscillator action and shows that beyond the first conjugate time neither occurs.

contents.name: Section 5.3, pages 148 onwards of the PDF pagination: applications of Euler's equation (shortest distance, catenary and related examples)
contents.reason: These applications are unconnected to the E19 verification claims and no item consumes them; the page keeps its scope to the second variation, parallel axis, two-mass modes and the pendulum bound.

contents.name: Section 14.2, pages 488-489 of the PDF pagination: two identical masses joined by identical outer springs and a coupling spring, with the secular determinant and two characteristic frequencies
contents.support: This is the second independent treatment of the two-mass system; the proposition states the eigenvalue relations and the exact frequencies with a complete proof.

contents.name: Section 14.3, pages 490-492 of the PDF pagination: normal modes and normal coordinates, rotated by 45 degrees in configuration space
contents.support: The proposition's in-phase and anti-phase eigenvectors (1,1)/sqrt2 and (1,-1)/sqrt2 are exactly those normal coordinates, derived here from the eigenrelations.

contents.name: Sections 14.4-14.5, pages 493 onwards of the PDF pagination: centre-of-mass oscillations and weak coupling
contents.reason: Centre-of-mass and weak-coupling approximations are not part of the E19 exact-mode computation, and the verification items make no perturbative claims.

sources.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 140, online edition)

contents.name: Section 2.4, printed pages 45-48: smooth dependence on initial conditions and the first variational equation
contents.support: The proposition instantiates the run's linearisation theorem, whose constants and hypotheses follow this treatment; the pendulum example evaluates them explicitly.

contents.name: Sections 6.2-6.3, printed pages 192-197: linearisation at equilibria and estimates comparing nonlinear and linear evolutions
contents.support: The example carries out the finite-time comparison of the nonlinear pendulum solution with the exactly harmonic linearised one at explicit constants.
